strengths: The paper targets a meaningful robustness problem: monocular depth models can interpret planar optical illusions as real geometry, with predictions changing when context is removed. The qualitative examples make this failure mode compelling.

The proposed dataset includes 468 source images, polygonal illusion annotations that exclude real objects, and context-restricted crops. This targeted resource could usefully complement conventional depth benchmarks.
The evaluation covers a broad range of depth models. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over the DAv2-L teacher: 93.5% lower DCS and 86.1% lower CCS.

The adaptation combines localized geometric supervision with background distillation. Component ablations demonstrate the importance of preserving non-ROI structure, and the NYUv2 ordinal results provide some evidence of retained general capability. The appendix also documents failure cases and degradation with extended training.
weaknesses: The central geometric premise is insufficiently justified. Sections 3–4 equate physical planarity with a near-zero image-space depth Laplacian and fit affine planes directly to predicted depth. Under perspective projection, inverse depth of a plane is affine, but metric depth generally is not. The evaluation mixes relative and metric models without specifying a common geometrically valid representation. Moreover, zero Laplacian does not imply an affine surface, and CCS can miss changes in plane slope or offset. Consequently, these metrics do not establish the claimed physical correctness or contextual consistency.

Generalization cannot be assessed from the reported protocol. The manuscript describes training on 3D-Mirage and evaluating on that benchmark, but gives no train/validation/test sizes or source-image-level separation. Although later figure captions mention a test set, the partition is undocumented. With multiple crops derived from each original image, explicit separation of originals and related scenes is essential to rule out leakage.

The metric definitions contain consequential inconsistencies. Equation 1 combines a norm of summed responses with a mean of per-pixel norms, yet Table 1 reports similarly sized components, with davg consistently exceeding dcluster; this is not explained by the stated sum-versus-mean definitions. Appendix A describes mean10 as the mean of the top decile, whereas Section 3.2 discards the lowest decile, and changes normalization from per-view to per-ROI. Crop registration, spatial resolution, and derivative scaling are also unspecified. These ambiguities prevent reproducing or confidently interpreting the main results.

Training directly suppresses the same Laplacian responses used for evaluation, so independent validation is particularly important. The paper lacks quantitative plane-reconstruction accuracy, validation against measured geometry, and controls distinguishing suppression of illusions from suppression of genuine protrusions. NYUv2 pairwise accuracy and teacher agreement on benchmark backgrounds are useful but insufficient to support the stronger claims of surgical correction and safety-relevant knowledge preservation. Appendix examples explicitly show that geometrically incorrect, low-variation predictions can receive favorable scores.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of the proposed method's complexity. Ablations remove entire HKR or NKP objectives but do not establish the contributions of the gated plane mixture, ring terms, dual-view training, or negative-data regularization relative to simpler plane-supervised adaptation. Figure 4 also describes full-image predictions matching a supposedly more accurate crop prediction, whereas the equations specify per-branch plane supervision and teacher preservation without that explicit cross-view objective. Important implementation details, including the gating inputs, plane count, ring construction, and several regularization weights, are missing.

Dataset provenance and annotation reliability need stronger documentation: collection sources, redistribution rights, deduplication, and procedures for verifying physical planarity are not provided. The contextual-cropping experiment also changes apparent scale and resampling alongside context, without controls separating these effects. Claims that global semantic priors cause the failure, and that the intervention establishes deployment robustness, therefore exceed the supplied evidence.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant robustness problem: monocular depth models can interpret planar optical illusions as actual geometry, with predictions changing under context removal. The qualitative examples across multiple model families motivate systematic investigation.

The collection of 468 source images with polygonal illusion annotations and context-restricted crops could become a useful diagnostic resource. Excluding real objects within illusion regions is a sensible annotation choice.

The adaptation combines localized geometric supervision with teacher-based background preservation. Table 2 provides useful evidence of the trade-off: the full method substantially lowers the proposed scores while retaining NYUv2 ordinal accuracy relatively closely (89.73% versus 90.13%). The supplementary failure examples and training-duration analysis are also informative.
weaknesses: The central geometric premise is not generally correct. Sections 3–4 equate physical planarity with a zero image-space depth Laplacian and fit affine functions of image coordinates to depth. Under perspective projection, inverse depth is affine for a plane; metric depth generally is not. The evaluation mixes relative and metric models without specifying a conversion that resolves this distinction. Moreover, a zero scalar Laplacian does not imply an affine surface. Consequently, the proposed objective and metrics do not establish physical planarity as claimed.

Generalization cannot be assessed from the reported protocol. The manuscript describes training on 3D-Mirage and evaluating on that benchmark, but gives no train/validation/test sizes or source-image-level separation procedure. Supplementary captions mention a test set without defining it. Since multiple crops originate from each source image, documenting separation before augmentation is essential. This omission leaves the headline improvements vulnerable to training-image or closely related crop overlap; it does not establish that leakage occurred, but prevents ruling it out.

The metric definitions and reported numbers are inconsistent. Equation 1 defines d_cluster using summed nonnegative Laplacian magnitudes and d_avg using their mean per-pixel vector magnitude. Under these definitions, d_avg cannot exceed d_cluster, yet every Table 1 row exhibits that ordering, including 505.8 versus 488.8 for DAv2-L. Appendix A also defines mean10 as the mean of the top decile, whereas Section 3.2 discards the bottom decile. Normalization changes from per-view to per-ROI between these descriptions. These discrepancies directly obstruct reproduction of the principal quantitative evidence.

DCS and CCS are insufficiently validated as measures of geometric correctness and contextual stability. Smoothing or predicting an incorrect affine surface can improve both; different affine predictions can have identical zero Laplacians despite substantial geometric disagreement. The appendix itself notes that structural collapse can improve scores. Because training directly suppresses the quantity used for evaluation, the reported 93.5% and 86.1% reductions need independent geometric validation, such as plane residuals in an appropriate 3D representation and checks of surface orientation and placement.

The experiments do not isolate the value of the proposed machinery. There are no controlled comparisons against simpler planar supervision or smoothing approaches, nor ablations of the gated plane mixture, ring terms, negative-image regularization, or dual-view training. NYUv2 ordinal accuracy and agreement with the teacher provide limited support for preservation: they do not establish depth accuracy or reliable retention of real obstacles in the targeted street setting. The claim that the model has learned to distinguish illusory texture from real geometry is therefore stronger than the evidence.

Several methodological and reporting inconsistencies further reduce confidence. Figure 4 describes matching the full-image student to a supposedly more accurate context-free crop prediction, unlike the plane-supervision losses in Section 4.3 and the paper's motivating observation. Table 2 and supplementary Table C report different one-epoch results for the no-preservation ablation. Dataset provenance, licensing, physical-planarity verification, gating-network specifications, and several training hyperparameters are missing. Assessed under the default Algorithms/General category while crediting the benchmark contribution, the unresolved metric validity and evaluation protocol are consequential shortcomings that prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant robustness problem: monocular depth models can interpret planar artwork as physical geometry, with failures worsening when context is removed. The examples across multiple model families make this a worthwhile computer-vision research direction.

The collection of 468 source images with planar-region annotations, exclusions for real objects, and context-restricted crops could provide a useful targeted benchmark beyond conventional depth datasets.

The adaptation strategy combines plausible components: parameter-efficient tuning, planar supervision, teacher-based background preservation, and ordinary-image regularization. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over DAv2-L: 93.5% in DCS and 86.1% in CCS.

The ablations explicitly examine the trade-off between suppressing illusions and preserving genuine geometry. NYUv2 ordinal accuracy remains close to the baseline, and the supplementary failure cases and training-duration analysis usefully acknowledge limitations.
weaknesses: The evaluation split is unspecified. Sections 3 and 5 do not give training, validation, and test counts or establish that all crops and related views of a source scene remain in one partition. Although later captions mention a test set, the manuscript does not establish that the reported adaptation gains measure generalization to unseen scenes. This is a major concern when training directly on the proposed benchmark.

The central geometric premise needs correction or qualification. Under perspective projection, metric depth on a tilted physical plane is generally reciprocal-affine in image coordinates, not affine; inverse depth is affine. Applying the same depth-space Laplacian criterion to metric and relative models without documenting representation conversion can penalize correct planes. Moreover, a zero scalar Laplacian does not imply planarity, and CCS can miss changes between different affine depth fields. These issues undermine interpreting the scores as physical geometric deviation and contextual consistency.

Metric definitions and implementation are insufficiently consistent. Section 3 defines mean10 by discarding the lowest 10%, whereas Appendix A calls it the mean of the top decile; normalization is described as per-view in the main text and per-ROI in the appendix. DCS combines a pixel sum with a pixel mean, creating an unexplained dependence on ROI size and resolution. Crop alignment, resampling, boundary treatment, and validation against independent geometric or human judgments are missing.

Because training directly suppresses the Laplacian quantity used for evaluation, large DCS/CCS improvements do not independently establish correct surface recovery. The appendix itself shows that geometrically incorrect flat patches can score favorably. Evaluation needs an independent geometric measure and targeted tests on genuine protrusions or obstacles. NYUv2 pairwise accuracy and background agreement with the teacher provide useful but limited evidence for the broad safety and knowledge-preservation claims.

The method description contains a substantive contradiction: Figure 4 describes matching the full-image ROI prediction to a supposedly more accurate context-free crop prediction, whereas Section 4.3 specifies teacher-neighborhood plane fitting and Laplacian regularization. The former also conflicts with the motivating observation that crops worsen hallucinations. Important details of plane fitting, gating, ring construction, and inference-time requirements remain unspecified, and simpler plane-supervision/distillation baselines are absent.

Several reporting and reproducibility issues require resolution. Table 2 and Appendix Table C give different one-epoch results for the no-preservation ablation; Appendix E's stated improvements disagree with Table A. Dataset provenance, licensing, annotation verification, and duplicate handling are not documented. Overall, under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the promising problem and qualitative evidence do not outweigh unresolved concerns about metric validity and held-out evaluation.
